passages.t: A mother's counsel to a king
passages.happening:
‘These are the words of King Lemuel’ (verse 1), taught to him by his mother. She begins with tenderness: ‘What shall I say, O my son? What, O son of my womb? What, O son of my vows?’ (verse 2).

She warns him: ‘Do not spend your strength on women or your vigor on those who ruin kings’ (verse 3). Kings must not crave wine and strong drink, ‘lest they drink and forget what is decreed, depriving all the oppressed of justice’ (verse 5). Let strong drink go instead to the one who is perishing, and wine to the bitter in soul, so that they forget their misery (verses 6-7).

And she gives him his task: “Open your mouth for those with no voice, for the cause of all the dispossessed. Open your mouth, judge righteously, and defend the cause of the poor and needy” (verses 8-9).
passages.hearers:
Lemuel is otherwise unknown. His name means something like belonging to God, and no king of Israel or Judah bore it. As in 30:1, the word massa in verse 1 may mean a weighty word, or it may name an Arabian people, making Lemuel king of Massa. If so, Proverbs includes wisdom from outside Israel, as it does in 22:17 to 24:22. Verse 2 even uses the Aramaic word bar for son, which some take as a sign of foreign origin.

This is the only part of Proverbs credited to a woman's teaching. The book that opened with a father teaching his son closes with a mother doing the same. In royal houses a king's mother often had real influence. In Judah the queen mother had an official place, and the books of Kings usually name the mother of each new king.

Her point about wine is a contrast. What dulls a ruler's judgment, and so harms the poor he is meant to protect, is set beside those whose lives are already full of misery. The king must stay clear-headed for their sake. These verses describe the misery of the poor. They are not advice to drown sorrow.

If drinking has become hard to control, you do not have to face it alone. Tell someone you trust, and reach out to a doctor or a recovery group near you. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.later: Lemuel's mother speaks like Hannah, who prayed for a son and vowed him to God (1 Samuel 1:11). The law gave the same warning to kings: ‘He must not take many wives for himself, lest his heart go astray’ (Deuteronomy 17:17). And the prophet gives the same charge as verse 9: ‘Defend the fatherless and plead the case of the widow’ (Isaiah 1:17).
passages.asks: A ruler's task is to speak for those who have no voice. Ask who around you has no voice, and where you could open your mouth for them. And ask what dulls your own judgment when others are depending on you.

passages.happening:
The book closes with a poem. “A wife of noble character, who can find? She is far more precious than rubies” (verse 10). ‘The heart of her husband trusts in her, and he lacks nothing of value’ (verse 11). ‘She brings him good and not harm all the days of her life’ (verse 12).

She chooses wool and flax and works with eager hands (verse 13). ‘She is like the merchant ships, bringing her food from afar’ (verse 14). She rises before dawn to provide for her household (verse 15). ‘She appraises a field and buys it; from her earnings she plants a vineyard’ (verse 16). ‘She girds herself with strength and shows that her arms are strong’ (verse 17).

She spins and weaves (verse 19). ‘She opens her arms to the poor and reaches out her hands to the needy’ (verse 20). When snow comes she does not fear for her household, for they are warmly clothed (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The poem is an acrostic. Each of its twenty-two verses begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, from first to last. The form suggests completeness, praise from A to Z.

Noble character translates eshet chayil, woman of strength. Chayil is used of warriors and armies, and the poem is full of heroic words: she girds herself with strength, her arms are strong, and the word behind ‘food’ in verse 15 more often means prey. It reads like a hymn usually sung for a warrior, sung here for a woman of everyday faithfulness. Boaz uses the same phrase of Ruth.

She works in the economy of an ancient household, where making cloth was a major part of women's work. She chooses wool and flax, spins with distaff and spindle, weaves, and sells to merchants. Scarlet and purple were costly dyes and fine linen a luxury. She buys a field and plants a vineyard with her earnings, which shows that women in such households could manage property and trade.
passages.later: Boaz says to Ruth, ‘all my fellow townspeople know that you are a woman of noble character’ (Ruth 3:11), the same words as verse 10. In some Hebrew traditions the book of Ruth follows Proverbs, as if to show a real woman of strength after the poem.
passages.asks: The poem praises strength used for others: household, neighbors, the poor. Ask how your own strength is being spent, and on whom. And ask whom you could honor this week for faithful work that usually goes unpraised.

passages.t: Strength and honor, and the fear of the LORD
passages.happening:
‘Her husband is known at the city gate, where he sits among the elders of the land’ (verse 23). She makes linen garments and sells them (verse 24). “Strength and honor are her clothing, and she can laugh at the days to come” (verse 25). ‘She opens her mouth with wisdom, and faithful instruction is on her tongue’ (verse 26). She watches over her household and does not eat the bread of idleness (verse 27).

Her children rise up and praise her, and her husband praises her too: many women have done noble things, but she surpasses them all (verses 28-29).

Then the poem's heart: “Charm is deceptive and beauty is fleeting, but a woman who fears the LORD is to be praised” (verse 30). ‘Give her the fruit of her hands, and let her works praise her at the gates’ (verse 31).
passages.hearers:
The gates were where a town's affairs were settled. Her husband sits there among the elders, and at the end her own works praise her in the same gates.

Faithful instruction in verse 26 is, in Hebrew, a teaching of chesed, loyal love. Her words carry the same steadfast love that marks God's covenant faithfulness.

Fleeting in verse 30 is hevel, breath or vapor, the key word of Ecclesiastes. The poem does not despise beauty. It says beauty does not last. What lasts is the fear of the LORD.

So Proverbs ends as it began. Its first chapters pictured Wisdom as a woman calling in the streets and building her house. Its last chapter shows a woman who builds up her household, speaks with wisdom and fears the LORD, the very thing the book called the beginning of knowledge in 1:7.
passages.later: The book's motto returns at its close: ‘The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge’ (Proverbs 1:7). And the psalm says to everyone who fears the LORD, ‘For when you eat the fruit of your labor, blessings and prosperity will be yours’ (Psalm 128:2).
passages.hard:
Is the woman of Proverbs 31 a model every wife must match?

Readers have understood the poem in several ways. Many take it as a portrait of an ideal wife, offered to young men as a picture of what to value in a spouse (verse 10 asks who can find her) and to women as a picture of godly strength. Others read it mainly as wisdom in person: the book began with Wisdom building her house (9:1), and it ends with a woman who builds up her household, so the poem shows what wisdom looks like when it is lived. Many hold both views, seeing a real woman who is the book's final portrait of wisdom lived out.

In Jewish homes the poem is traditionally sung by husbands to their wives at the Sabbath meal, as praise and not as a checklist.

Whatever reading one takes, the poem is praise, not a performance standard. Its twenty-two verses gather many kinds of excellence into one picture, and it would misuse the poem to turn it into a burden no woman can carry. It does not measure any woman by her marriage, her children, her income or her energy.

Its heart is verse 30. What makes her worth praising is not charm, beauty or achievement but the fear of the LORD, and that is open to every believer, married or single, woman or man.
passages.asks: The poem ends by praising a woman who fears the LORD. Ask whom in your life you could praise, out loud, for faithfulness you have taken for granted. And ask what it would mean for you, whoever you are, to make the fear of the LORD your strength and your clothing.
